analysis.title: How much runway is left in the data center construction cycle?
key_insights: GS sees good visibility into continued US data center construction spending growth through 2028 from projects already under construction and from announced projects Aterio rates high probability. Visibility is more limited beyond 2028.

About 86 GW of data centers are under construction. At ~$3.5 bn construction spend per GW (Census Bureau scope, excludes servers, racks, GPUs and network equipment), that is ~$300 bn, about 6x 2025 US data center construction spending of ~$50 bn.
Adding high-probability announcements expands the pipeline TAM to ~$900 bn. The full pipeline of ~550 GW is worth ~$1.9 tn, which measures total pipeline value rather than expected spend.

Projects under construction support double-digit construction spending growth in 2027, reaching ~$105 bn, and underpin roughly half of GS's 2028 spending forecast. Beyond 2027, growth depends on announced projects that have not yet started.

There are >171 GW of high-probability announced projects not yet in construction (~37% of announcements). Aterio says about 80% of high-probability projects are historically energized. Applying that rate moves the spending peak from 2027 to 2028, with 2027 spend up ~$50 bn to ~$155 bn and 2028 up ~$105 bn to ~$185 bn.

On current timelines, spending on the existing pipeline peaks in 2028 but stays above 2026 levels through 2030. The ~293 GW of medium and low probability projects could extend the cycle. Treating them as energizing on schedule would put the peak in 2029, which GS calls unrealistic.

GS raises its data center construction spending forecasts for 2026/2027 to $80 bn/$100 bn from $67 bn/$87 bn and introduces a 2028 forecast of $125 bn. Spending growth accelerated from 55% yoy in June to 90% yoy in September, and 3Q construction starts were up meaningfully yoy.

GS economists expect Democratic governors in Texas, Georgia and Michigan to impose conditional moratoria on new data center development pending legislation. These states are ~45% of planned US capacity, with Texas ~25%. GS sees this as a timing risk that smooths spending and extends the cycle rather than cutting the TAM.

Moratoria mainly affect projects not yet started, and GS does not assume projects under construction are halted. Current timelines imply ~55 GW energizing in 2028, well above the historical pace, and GS already viewed them as aggressive before the election.
For GS's data center construction coverage (FIX, EME, LGN), bookings follow project starts by roughly six months, which buffers against pauses in new project development.

Signals GS is watching: project starts (construction takes ~2 years), incremental announcements (~1 year from announcement to construction start, up 55% yoy), and conversion of announced projects into Aterio's high-probability category (~171 GW of ~464 GW today).

The demand backdrop: hyperscaler capex is on track for ~$800 bn in 2026 with FactSet consensus ~$1.3 tn in 2027. The three largest public cloud providers have announced a combined >$1.7 tn of revenue backlog.

tension_points.bull_case: Projects under construction (~86 GW, ~$300 bn) and high-probability announcements support double-digit spending growth through 2028. A ~293 GW medium and low probability pipeline could extend the cycle to 2029-2030 and beyond.
tension_points.bear_case: On current timelines spending on the existing pipeline peaks in 2028. Midterm-driven moratoria in Texas, Georgia and Michigan, and aggressive timelines (~55 GW energizing in 2028), could delay projects.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence that high-probability 2027 to 2028 delivery timelines are shifting right with cancellation, or a slowdown in project announcements and in medium and low probability projects progressing to high probability, would undercut the 2029-2030 extension case.

theme_stances.key_argument: Projects under construction and high-probability announcements give visibility into continued spending growth through 2028, and midterm moratoria are more likely to shift timing than cut demand.
theme_stances.evidence: good visibility into continued US data center construction spending growth through 2028

theme_stances.key_argument: State-level moratoria are expected to be conditional and short-lived and mainly affect projects not yet started.
theme_stances.evidence: midterms results are more likely to shift the timing of spending than change underlying demand
